terms.definition: A defender lined up head-up (directly) over the center.
A defensive lineman aligned shaded on a shoulder of the center, in an A gap.
A defender lined up head-up on an offensive guard.
A defender lined up on the inside shoulder of an offensive guard.
A one-gap 3-4 front shifted to the closed (tight end) side: the nose in a 0 shade or 1-technique toward the tight end, the open-side end in a 2- or 3-technique.
An interior defensive lineman aligned on the outside shoulder of the offensive guard, aiming at the B gap; in a 4-3 he is the quick penetrating tackle.
The back-end coverage behind a five-man fire zone: three defenders deep and three underneath.
A defender lined up head-up on an offensive tackle (a 4i is the inside-shoulder version).

A 4-3 variation developed by Buddy Ryan for the Chicago Bears that crowds the line with six players and puts eight in the box; the line is shifted toward the offense's weak side and three defensive backs crowd the line. Named after Bears strong safety Doug Plank's jersey number.
A defender lined up on the inside shoulder of an offensive tackle.
A pass rush of five defenders, one more than the usual four.
A defensive lineman aligned on the offensive tackle (outside shade in most sources); the standard end in a 3-4 front.
A defender lined up head-up on a tight end.
A defender lined up on the inside shoulder of a tight end.
A defender lined up outside the tight end (or the last blocker on the line), at least a half yard outside his outside shoulder.
The gap between the center and a guard; there is one on each side.
The gap between an offensive guard and tackle.
A corner's technique of turning and sinking backward at the snap, often from a press alignment, to get depth for the deep zone.
A hybrid defensive end/linebacker rush role used by some defenses, mostly in college; the label is a team playbook name, not one fixed position.
A man-coverage call used against stacked, bunched or slot receivers in which defenders switch assignments by what the receivers do.
A front that puts defenders on the center and both guards (head up) to clog the interior gaps.
A strong-side defensive end, typically 280+ pounds, who stops the run on base downs and moves inside to tackle on passing downs; used by Seattle, Denver, Cincinnati and Las Vegas.
A defensive call that sends extra rushers, usually linebackers or defensive backs, after the quarterback beyond the normal four-man line rush.
The cornerback who plays to the short side of the field (the boundary), often a bigger, more physical jam corner.
The area on the defensive side of the ball within about five yards of the line and framed by the offensive tackles, where run defenders line up.
Two defenders, usually one underneath/inside and one over the top/outside, take away one receiver together.
A name for a pass-rushing edge/outside linebacker, often the weak-side or boundary rusher; some defenses use Buck and Jack as two different edge roles.
A power move where the rusher drives straight into the blocker's chest and tries to push him back into the quarterback.
Man coverage where the corner lines up tight on the receiver and jams him at the line.
The gap between an offensive tackle and the tight end (outside the tackle).
A defender stays with a receiver running vertically through his zone, often until handing him to a deeper defender.
A rush move where the rusher strikes (clubs) the blocker's shoulder or arm with a forearm or hand to knock him off balance before getting past.
A man coverage in which two defenders work together on a star receiver, such as double coverage.
A Saban pattern-match coverage call, like Dog but with the corner's leverage inverted: the corner takes outside leverage with a safety bracketing inside.
A defensive assignment to keep the ball carrier from getting to the edge and turning upfield, usually given to an outside linebacker or cornerback.
A rusher told to hold the outside lane so the quarterback cannot run past him outside the pocket.
A rush by a cornerback.
A defensive back who lines up across from a wide receiver, mainly to cover him and break up passes, and who also supports against the run.
Pure man coverage with no deep safety help, usually paired with a blitz.
Man coverage on every eligible receiver with one deep safety helping over the top.
Cover 1 with a 'rat', an underneath defender (often the end opposite the pressure or a linebacker) who acts as a vision dropper in the middle; the '1' in Cover 1 signals a rat in the coverage.
A zone coverage with two deep safeties each covering a deep half, corners usually jamming at the line and sinking, and five defenders underneath.
Two safeties deep in halves with man-to-man coverage underneath on every receiver.
A zone coverage with three deep defenders (two corners and a safety), each covering a third of the deep field, with four defenders underneath.
A Cover 3 variation where one corner rolls to the flat and two safeties cover the three deep zones with the other corner.
A zone-based coverage with four deep defenders each responsible for a quarter of the deep field and three underneath, using man-to-man principles and bracketing the number-one receivers.
A split-field coverage that plays quarters (Cover 4) on one side and Cover 2 on the other.
A defensive end charging hard into the backfield instead of staying wide.
A zone-coverage assignment where the defender buzzes the curl area and then widens to the flat; usually the strong safety and a linebacker or nickel in Cover 3.
The space between a defender and the receiver at the snap.
A Saban call used against balanced 2x2 formations in which the corner jams the first receiver breaking outside and the apex handles the second receiver if he goes vertical.
The gap outside the tight end (the opposite side from the tackle).
One of the four deep zones in Cover 4; each deep defender is responsible for a quarter of the deep field.
The half of the field behind the underneath coverage that a safety covers in Cover 2.
The deep center of the field, covered by a free safety in man-free and Cover 3.
One of the three deep zones of the field that a defender covers in Cover 3.
A cornerback or safety, the players who defend the pass behind the linebackers.
A lineman on an outside end of the defensive line who rushes the passer and contains or stops runs to his side.
An interior defensive lineman who lines up opposite the offensive guards and tries to stop the run and disrupt the play in the backfield.
The zone blitz, in which a pass rusher drops into coverage while another defender rushes; LeBeau refined and popularized it.
A dime package of four linemen, one linebacker and six defensive backs (numbers are linemen, linebackers, backs).
The sixth defensive back on the field, added in obvious passing situations; named because a dime is worth two nickels.
Showing a coverage look before the snap that differs from the coverage actually played.
A 3-4 one-gap front where both ends align in a 4i (inside shoulder of the tackle) and play the B gap, the nose works to the front side A gap, and the Sam plays a two-gap technique over the tight end.
A defender whose main job is attacking the quarterback from the outside edge of the offensive line: a defensive end in a four-man front or an outside linebacker in a three-man front.
Eight defenders in the box, which happens when a safety moves down to help against the run.
A 4-3 base look with no nose tackle, a left and right tackle instead.
The wide side (field) and the short side (boundary) of the field, used to align players and calls.
The wide side of the field is 'the field' and the short side is 'the boundary'; defenses set strengths and positions (field corner, boundary corner) by these sides.
The cornerback who lines up on the wide side of the field (the field), as opposed to the boundary corner on the short side.
To step up and take a gap or area to stop a run, often a safety or linebacker filling a gap vacated by a lineman.
A zone blitz that sends five rushers with three deep and three under defenders behind it.
The area near the sideline close to the line of scrimmage, the underneath outside zone.
The defender who is responsible for the edge on a run play, keeping the ball carrier from turning the corner and forcing him back inside to pursuit.
The safety who lines up deeper, is free to roam and follow the ball, and is the last man back on pass plays.
The defensive linemen and linebackers together.
The space between two offensive linemen, lettered A through D from the center outward, that a defender can be assigned to control.
A pass-rush move where the rusher baits the blocker's punch, ducks under it and turns the corner.
Lining up directly across from a blocker, nose to nose.
A name for a hybrid defensive back used in some programs; Penn State's Rip Engle gave the name to his strong safety position.
The underneath zone between the hash marks about ten yards deep, covered by linebackers.
A defender lined up on the inside shoulder of the receiver, taking away inside-breaking routes by alignment and using the sideline as help.
A linebacker aligned inside, between the outside linebackers, in a 3-4 (two ILBs) or as the middle linebacker.
A coverage where a safety drops underneath into the box while a corner plays the deep half, the reverse of normal roles.

A linebacker name whose meaning depends on the system. Most sources use it for the 3-4 outside linebacker or end who is the primary edge pass rusher and may line up on either side; Bowen and the Wikipedia glossary use it for the weak-side inside linebacker of a 3-4.
Using the hands to make contact with a receiver and disrupt his route at the line of scrimmage.
A hybrid defensive end/outside linebacker in the Seahawks-style 4-3 Under who rushes from the weak side, usually standing up, in a one-gap technique.
A defender who lines up behind the defensive line and can stop the run, rush the passer or drop into pass coverage.
A blitz by a linebacker, the most common kind.
A call that puts a corner in off-man coverage on one receiver, often the backside X of a 3x1 formation, with no inside help so the safety can help elsewhere.
A Cover 1 tag on a four-man rush that makes the linebacker opposite the running back the free 'vision dropper' sitting underneath; coaches reverse lurk and hole.
A pass coverage in which each defender is assigned to a specific offensive player.
Man-to-man coverage on the receivers with one free safety playing deep middle.
Close man-to-man coverage on a receiver, as in bump-and-run.
A zone-based coverage in which defenders switch to man on a receiver based on the route he runs.
Man Everywhere he Goes: a man-match Quarters call in which a defender stays on his receiver wherever he goes.
The linebacker the defense treats as its middle linebacker: in a 4-3 the middle man who relays the call and sets the front, in a 3-4 the stronger, larger inside linebacker.
A Tite-based front that walks a Jack linebacker onto the edge.
A name for the weak-side interior linebacker of a 3-4, the same player the Wikipedia glossary also calls Jack.
Short for 'Man On Demand', the core of Saban's man-match system: a defender attaches to a receiver only on a route over five yards, otherwise he plays zone and passes the receiver off.
Short for 'middle of the field open': coverages with two deep safeties, so the deep middle is not guarded by one player (versus MOFC, middle of the field closed, one deep safety).
The name some teams use for the sixth defensive back in a dime package.
A strong safety given free rein to play the run, cover or rush the passer.
Monte Kiffin's Tampa Cover 2 scheme out of a 4-3 front.
The nickel base look with four linemen, two linebackers and five defensive backs.
A fifth defensive back who comes on in passing situations, usually in place of a linebacker.
The defensive lineman who lines up over or across from the center, the middle man of a three-man front, usually tying up blockers to protect linebackers.
A defensive front with an odd number of down linemen, most often three (a 3-4).
A defender lines up several yards off the receiver, giving him a cushion.
A 3-4 front descended from the 5-2 Oklahoma defense.
A technique where a lineman is responsible for attacking one gap, instead of holding two.
Lining up on the outside shoulder of the player across from you; a defender with 'outside leverage' aligns on the outside eye of the receiver.
Lining up on the outside shoulder of the receiver to force him inside.
A linebacker aligned outside the box tackles: responsible for outside containment, blitzing and covering the flats; in a 3-4 he is often the main edge rusher.
A 4-3 front shifted to the strong (tight end, closed) side: the 3-technique tackle lines up on the strong side and the nose on the weak side in a 0 shade or 2i.
A split-field coverage from a Cover 2 look where the corner reads the number-two receiver's release and jumps the first outside route, with a safety deep over the top; also called 2-Trap.
Defending against passing plays through coverage and pass rush.
The defenders' effort to reach and pressure the quarterback on a pass play, usually by the four down linemen plus any blitzers.
The side of the formation with the most passing threats, where the defense adds a coverage player.
A zone-looking coverage in which defenders switch to man-style responsibilities based on how the receivers' routes develop.
A defender moving backward with short, quick steps while keeping his eyes on the receiver or quarterback.
To charge through a gap into the backfield with speed and quickness to disrupt the play, as the 3-technique and rush end do in a 4-3.
The 4-3 Under, Leo end and Cover 3 with a safety dropping near linebacker depth, put together by Pete Carroll and Dan Quinn at Seattle.
To close a gap, often a lineman holding it against a run while linebackers flow around him.
A safety on the back side of a coverage helps on the front side.
The area behind the offensive line created by pass blockers where the quarterback stands to throw.
A defender lines up on the receiver at the line to jam him and disrupt the route at the snap.
A deep zone defense, used to protect a lead late in a half or game, that gives up short gains to stop long ones.
An old term for a linebacker rush that made six rushers against five blockers.
A Saban-originated Cover 3 match call: rip or liz tells which way the safety rotates (to the right or left), and the match rules handle the receivers, especially against four verticals.
A pass-rush move where the rusher drives his inside arm up under the blocker's arm to win leverage.
A safety (sometimes a linebacker) who starts deep or shows another coverage, then drops into the underneath middle of the field in man-free coverage to undercut crossing, slant, in and dig routes.
Changing the coverage after the snap from the look shown before it.
Moving the safeties (and sometimes corners) before or after the snap so the coverage shell changes, often to disguise it.
A hybrid safety-linebacker used near the line who has both defensive back and linebacker duties; the name is more common in college than the NFL.
The side of the offensive formation where the tight end lines up (or that has the most blockers), toward which the defense sets its run strength.
Nick Saban's system of pattern-matching coverage, in which defenders use rules based on what routes do to decide whom to cover rather than only spot-dropping or playing straight man.
A tackle of the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage before he throws.
A blitz in which a safety, usually the free safety, rushes the passer.
The strong-side linebacker, who lines up on the tight end's side and has to handle the tight end and edge run plays.
The vertical lane between the hashes (and the zone defenders), where vertical routes up the middle run; a defender 'runs the seam' to carry it.
A Cover 3 with a safety dropping to about linebacker depth, putting eight defenders near the line.
The defensive backs as a group, the cornerbacks and safeties, mainly responsible for pass coverage.
To hold outside leverage against the blocker so the runner cannot get outside the tackle and is funneled back inside.
Lining up on one shoulder of a blocker instead of head-up.
A defender charging into a gap at the snap.
A shell with one safety deep in the middle of the field, as in Cover 1 and Cover 3.
A quick inside-breaking route: a receiver takes a few steps upfield then cuts across the field at about 45 degrees.
The area between the split end and the rest of the offensive line, or the receiver aligned there; defenses cover it with a nickel or slot corner.
To force a runner outside, toward pursuit help, instead of letting him cut up inside.
A rotation where a safety spins down toward the line or flat after the snap while the other safety or a corner takes the deep area.
A pass-rush move where the rusher turns a full circle past the blocker.
A defender who neither rushes nor drops into a normal zone, but watches and mirrors a mobile quarterback to stop scrambles.
A look where linebackers line up behind the down linemen; Bowen names the 4-3 Over linebacker look 'tan-zero-tan' (tackle, zero technique, tackle).

A defensive end or rush linebacker who plays from a standing two-point stance; Wikipedia's Defensive end page also uses the term for the traditional containment-style end who waits rather than crashes inside.
Saban's name for the nickel (fifth DB) slot hybrid, a cornerback-sized slot defender who also plays the run.
The defense's call naming its strong side, normally the side of the tight end (run strength).
The safety who lines up on the strong side (the tight end side), plays closer to the line than the free safety, and helps against the run.
The side of the offense with the tight end, or with the most players if there is no tight end or more than one.

A split-field coverage against a 3x1 (three-receiver) side in which the corner presses the number-one receiver in man, a defender takes number two man-to-man unless number three goes to the flat, and the safety takes number three vertically or brackets number two.
A tackle of a ball carrier on a running play behind the line of scrimmage.
A pass-rush move where two rushers exchange paths so one blocker is picked or screened and a rusher gets free; a twist is the stunt where the two cross.
A rush move where the rusher grabs or pulls the blocker's shoulder or jersey and swings an arm over the top to get past him.

The area in the offensive backfield between the two offensive tackles; NCAA rules define it as a rectangle bounded by the neutral zone, lines five yards each side of the snapper and the offense's end line.
A tackle of a ball carrier behind the line of scrimmage, costing the offense yardage.
The middle linebacker in the Tampa 2 who runs deep down the middle behind the underneath linebackers.
A Cover 2 zone in which the middle linebacker runs the deep middle seam, giving a three-deep look behind two deep safeties; built from a 4-3 front.
A compressed front with a nose tackle over the center and the ends in 4i alignments, mainly used to defend spread offenses and cover B gaps.
A defender plays behind and outside the receiver, keeping him in front or to the inside.
A formation with three receivers lined up to one side.

A Saban-system call for defending the single receiver on the backside of a 3x1 set: the safety spins down to the curl/flat, and the corner either stays in man-on-the-edge or inverts to the deep half, giving a Cover 6 look.
A line stunt in which two rushers swap paths, one looping around behind the other.
A technique where a lineman controls the blocker and is responsible for two gaps, letting linebackers run free; used by 3-4 ends and nose tackles.
A defense that plays two safeties deep.
A defense with only two levels of defenders (line and one back level) instead of the usual three; usually more aggressive.
A 4-3 front where the nose tackle sits on the closed (tight end) side and the 3-technique to the open side, the opposite of the Over front.
A one-gap 3-4 front (the 3-4 Under) run by Wade Phillips with the Texans.
A linebacker or defender aligned at the line of scrimmage rather than behind it.
To 'wall off' a route: a middle-hook defender closes off inside-breaking and crossing routes underneath.
The side of the formation away from the tight end (or with the fewest offensive players on or near the line); the opposite of the strong side.
A front where the defensive ends line up very wide of the offensive tackle, in a 9-technique, to rush the edge; the name became popular after the Eagles.
The weak-side linebacker, the one who lines up away from the tight end; in a 4-3 usually the fastest of the three linebackers.
A blitz run out of Cover 0: more rushers than the offense has blockers, every receiver covered man-to-man and no deep safety.
A rush of five or more in which one or more players who normally rush (often a lineman or edge) drop into coverage while other defenders rush, behind a zone coverage.
Pass coverage in which each defender covers an area of the field rather than a specific receiver.
